claims.text: Transferring from entailment data is more effective for natural yes/no question answering than transferring from paraphrase or extractive QA data.
Transferring from entailment data continues to improve performance even when starting from pre-trained language models such as BERT.
Training BERT on MultiNLI and then fine-tuning on the BoolQ dataset achieves 80.43% test accuracy.
Human annotators achieve 90% accuracy on the BoolQ dataset.
Asking human annotators directly to write NLI candidate statements results in examples that typically only require surface-level reasoning.
Training a recurrent model on the BoolQ train set alone yields 69.60% dev accuracy.

evidence.description: MultiNLI transfer reached 75.57% dev accuracy compared to 71.36% for QNLI (extractive QA) and 71.30% for QQP (paraphrasing) using the same recurrent architecture.
Pre-trained BERT-Large with MultiNLI fine-tuning achieves 80.43% test accuracy compared to 76.70% for pre-trained BERT-Large without MultiNLI pre-training.
Our best method trains BERT on MultiNLI and then re-trains it on our train set. It achieves 80.4% accuracy compared to 90% accuracy of human annotators.
On the 110 selected gold-standard examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels.
Evidence cited from Gururangan et al. (2018), Jia and Liang (2017), and McCoy et al. (2019) showing crowd workers introduce surface-level artifacts when prompted to generate statements.
Table 3 reports Recurrent model accuracy on BoolQ dev set with no transfer data as 69.60%.

methodologies.name: BoolQ Dataset Construction
methodologies.description: Collection of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions from unprompted Google search queries, paired with Wikipedia passages and human-annotated yes/no answers.
conditions: unprompted search queries starting with yes/no indicator words
human annotation for answerability and yes/no label

methodologies.name: Two-Step Transfer Learning with BERT
methodologies.description: Fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT-Large model on MultiNLI entailment data prior to fine-tuning on the BoolQ target task.

limitations.text: Direct crowd-worker statement generation in prior NLI datasets results in artifacts that require only surface-level reasoning.
Existing yes/no QA subsets in datasets like QuAC heavily prompt users and feature class imbalance (e.g., 80% 'yes' answers).
Training neural models on the BoolQ dataset without pre-training or transfer learning yields accuracy only slightly above the majority baseline.
Gathering naturally occurring questions paired with document passages requires annotators to read entire Wikipedia articles, making annotation expensive.

future_work.text: Building a document-level version of the yes/no question answering task to increase difficulty and realism for real-world application.
Exploring pre-training on several intermediate tasks in succession or via multi-task learning before fine-tuning on yes/no QA.
